questions.stem: A two-way table shows: Boys who walk = 15, Boys who cycle = 10, Girls who walk = 20, Girls who cycle = 5. A student is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student is a girl who cycles?
questions.explanation: Total students = 15 + 10 + 20 + 5 = 50. P(girl who cycles) = 5/50 = 1/10. A common error is dividing by just the girls (25) or just the cyclists (15).

questions.stem: From the same table (Boys: walk 15, cycle 10; Girls: walk 20, cycle 5), given that a student walks, what is the probability the student is a boy?
questions.explanation: Given the student walks, we restrict to walkers only: 15 boys + 20 girls = 35 walkers. P(boy | walks) = 15/35 = 3/7. Option (a) doesn't restrict to walkers. Option (b) restricts to boys instead.

questions.stem: A survey of 120 students asked about pets. Cat owners: 35, Dog owners: 45, Both: 15, Neither: 55. How many students own a cat but NOT a dog?
questions.explanation: Cat only = Total cat owners − Both = 35 − 15 = 20. The 35 cat owners includes the 15 who also own dogs, so we must subtract those.

questions.stem: In a two-way table: Year 10 chose French = 24, Spanish = 16; Year 11 chose French = 18, Spanish = 22. What percentage of all students chose Spanish?
A two-way table has missing values. Men: Tea = 28, Coffee = ?, Total = 50. Women: Tea = ?, Coffee = 35, Total = 60. Total: Tea = ?, Coffee = ?, Grand total = 110. How many women prefer tea?
questions.explanation: Men coffee = 50 − 28 = 22. Women tea = 60 − 35 = 25. Verify: Total tea = 28 + 25 = 53, Total coffee = 22 + 35 = 57, Grand total = 53 + 57 = 110. Correct.
